sections.name: Hammer
sections.card:
Summary: A close-range item from the Donkey Kong arcade game. Whoever grabs it swings nonstop, and its knockback is extremely strong and vertical.
Uses: Swings do heavy damage and knockback. Holders cannot guard, use specials or jump again in the air, so a ledge knock-off can KO them.
Tips: From Melee on, one pickup in eight loses the head. Once it falls off, the head makes a strong throwing item.

sections.name: Beam Sword
sections.card:
Summary: A battering item with long reach, nicknamed the lightsaber because it looks like one. Holding it adds power, and you can charge it or throw it.
Tips: Its reach grows most on charged smashes in Melee. Peach can pull one out with Vegetable, but the Melee odds are 1/768.

sections.name: Star Rod
sections.card:
Summary: An odd mix of battering item and projectile item, loaded with sixteen stars. Thrown, it hits with strong semi-spike knockback.
Uses: Swing it for close hits, or use a smash or tilt to fire stars. Falcon's forward smash fires 5 stars at once and Sheik's fires 2.
Tips: Once empty, throwing it is the more practical choice: the semi-spike can ruin a recovery or act as a KO. Reflecting or absorbing moves can stop its stars.

sections.name: Super Scope
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range shooting item modelled on an actual Nintendo accessory. In Melee a tap fires three small shots, and holding the button charges a bigger one.
Uses: Mash the button for a stream of weak shots that leave foes almost no time to act. A bigger charge costs more of Melee's 48 shots.
Tips: Uncharged shots pass through foes, so one burst can trap several. Their 280 degree angle makes a weak meteor smash, and an empty Scope only puffs smoke.

sections.name: Ray Gun
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range weapon whose sideways knockback makes it easy to juggle foes at low percents.
Uses: It holds 16 shots, each doing 4% in Melee, and can fire once every 30 frames. At middle percents the sideways push carries foes to the blast line.
Tips: A reflector can send back both the shots and a thrown gun, while an absorber only works on the shots.

sections.name: Maxim Tomato and Heart Container
sections.card:
Summary: Two items that heal: either one lowers the damage percentage of whoever grabs it. In Melee a Maxim Tomato takes 50% off, and a Heart Container takes off 100% in total.
Uses: Damage you take while a Maxim Tomato heals comes off what it restores, so a 10% hit leaves only 40% healed.
Looks like: A little red tomato with an M, in black and white, on its front.
Tips: The All-Star Rest Area hands you three Heart Containers, and these heal every point of your damage, not just 100%. A glitch in Melee cuts a Heart Container's healing short if you step into the teleporter, so you are not fully healed.

sections.name: Metal Box
sections.card:
Summary: First seen in Melee, this item makes whoever smashes it become a Metal fighter for a short while. Metal fighters are far heavier and walk more slowly, but fall faster.
Uses: The effect lasts 12 seconds in Melee, but damage shortens it, fire attacks most of all. Your walking speed is multiplied by 0.7 and your jump force by 1.55, which is usually not enough to offset how fast you fall.
Tips: Falling faster makes it harder to get back to the stage. In Melee a Metal Box vanishes if a projectile touches it, but disjointed attacks, and any hit from a character wielding a sword, still break it and still make the attacker metal.

sections.name: Super Star (Starman)
sections.card:
Summary: A Mario item, called the Starman in Melee, that gives you ten seconds of invincibility.
Uses: Melee copies the first game here: running into foes does not damage them.
Looks like: The fighter who takes it sparkles brightly.
Tips: It ricochets in big arcs over the field, off platforms and walls, and it can fall off the stage if nobody grabs it in time. In Melee, the star's own tune pushes the stage music down until you can barely hear it.

sections.name: Super Mushroom and Poison Mushroom
sections.card:
Summary: Two Mario items that change your size for about ten seconds. The Super Mushroom, new in Melee, makes you bigger, and the Poison Mushroom shrinks you.
Uses: In Melee a Super Mushroom multiplies your weight by 1.6 and direct-attack damage by 1.2, but gives no armor. A Poison Mushroom does the reverse, shrinking you and cutting weight and attack damage.
Looks like: You can tell the Poison Mushroom from a Super Mushroom by its angry eyes and duller colours.
Tips: Both mushrooms drift rightward after they appear, though in Melee one that appears on the stage's right side drifts left instead. If you touch one while the other is working on you, you go back to normal size. In Melee, if you jump just as a Super Mushroom runs out, you get a super jump about the height of two jumps taken in a Bunny Hood.

sections.name: Fighting Wire Frames
sections.card:
Summary: Enemies you meet often in Melee's single-player modes, with male and female versions. They are mostly weak, light fighters who go down very easily.
Weak points: They cannot charge smash attacks, and with no special moves they rely on high jumps to get back. Their attacks are much weaker copies of Captain Falcon's and Zelda's.
Looks like: Pink lines forming the outline of a person. The face bears the logo of Super Smash Bros. and the chest holds something red shaped like a heart. They are bigger than the fighters they copy.
Tips: Males always chase after your character, while females hang back and seldom go straight for you. In Cruel Melee every one of them is fiercely aggressive, hits very hard and is tougher to knock off the stage, so surviving among them is hard. In Adventure Mode you fight them on a Battlefield with low gravity, and there and in Multi-Man Melee neither Star KOs nor Screen KOs work on them.

sections.name: Classic Mode's final boss
sections.card:
Summary: The closing fight of Classic Mode, set on Melee's Final Destination. You win by draining a fixed amount of HP, and in Melee how much depends on the difficulty.
Weak points: In Melee this boss can no longer turn around. Where it moves is set wholly by the attack it is performing and where you stand, and between attacks it goes back to where it started.
Looks like: A glove. In Melee the wrist just fades out instead of ending at a cuff.
Tips: It gets stronger at each difficulty step, and the top levels give it a lot of attacks that can finish you in one hit. A laser leaves each of its fingertips. When it makes a gun shape, it fires one pair of bullets until it has taken 150% damage, and three pairs after that. Its ground slap buries a player; its ground throw cannot normally KO, though it deals big damage and knockback. On Normal or harder, if you take off half its HP within 5 minutes 50 seconds of Classic Mode starting, a second boss joins the fight.

sections.name: A hidden boss in Classic Mode
sections.card:
Summary: A bonus boss that can join Classic Mode's last fight alongside the final boss, but only when the conditions the game sets for it are met.
Weak points: Its HP at the start is the same as the first boss's. When it lies on the floor and thrashes, that attack cannot reach anyone in the air, and any bomb it drops that hits a character before landing deals little damage and almost no knockback.
Looks like: It looks just like the final boss, except that it is a left hand.
Tips: Most of its moves are beefed-up versions of the final boss's, with a few that are its own. The fist it flies in with from behind the stage can star KO from as little as 35%, its forward throw can KO at low damage if you do not use DI, and the last of its three pokes can star KO at mid to high percentages.

sections.name: Brinstar's rising acid
sections.card:
Summary: Every so often a quake shakes Brinstar and acid begins to climb, at times submerging part of the stage. It does damage and medium knockback, and it takes a very high percent before it can KO, although in Melee a glitch with the ceiling lets it KO at extremely low percents.
Looks like: Yellow acid, with a large pool of it in the background under a brain-like creature.
Tips: While it climbs, it generally stops anyone being KO'd off the lowest blast line. It climbs and halts at irregular spacing, seldom reaches its peak, where everything but the highest platform is covered, and after a while it drains away. Grabbing the Super Star lets a character avoid it. Attacks can wear down the fleshy parts that hold the stage together, and while they regrow you can drop through them. In Melee, touching the acid makes a distinctive splash and a sizzling sound.

sections.name: F-Zero racers on Mute City
sections.card:
Summary: Thirty F-Zero Racers act as a hazard on Mute City. They keep driving around the track, though they appear only on some stretches of it, and only at certain times and on certain laps. Touching one hurts and sends you upward.
Weak points: Racers can be hurt, and even blown up, by explosives like the Motion-Sensor Bomb, by strong attacks, by items such as the Home-Run Bat and the Hammer, and by stationary Pokémon such as Venusaur or Charizard.
Tips: A racer that is destroyed leaves its wreck lying where it blew up until the match ends. If the platform is floating above the track and you touch the track, you take damage too. On Adventure Mode's F-Zero stage, a large "!" appears on screen as cars approach, each hit costs 35%, and pink platforms along the track can be hopped onto to stay clear.

sections.name: Pokémon Stadium's changing terrain
sections.card:
Summary: At irregular intervals the stage turns into one of four variants picked at random, each themed on a Pokémon type, then goes back to normal and starts over. The same variant can come up two times running.
Looks like: The normal stage is symmetrical: one big main platform with two soft platforms hovering over it. Behind it you see a huge jumbotron, a crowd and fireworks.
Tips: The big screen shows a symbol of the coming variant while the stage is changing. In Melee tournaments, many players wait through the Fire and Rock forms by staying on the far side of the stage from their opponent until it returns to normal, and many say this wastes time. On the Fire variant in Melee, a character hit toward the right of the tree's base may fall through. The flames behind the Fire variant are decoration only. On the Water variant's windmill, whoever stands on the lowest arm falls, and in Melee its arms are soft.
